about: The Orthogonal technology table for one job, light at night, and what it needs. Read by orthogonal/grow.js (CAF after Hordijk 2023, the keep rule after Arthur and Polak 2006, with 'better' measured by Nordhaus 1996's price of light, the measure block below); the same table grows every world, and only the endowment changes. A row's jobs are what it makes; inputs are consumed, every one needed; tools are catalysts, any one enough. Each Earth row is the version that came into general use, as the ledger records light in use (the sources of the brief's ledger are Fouquet and Pearson's), with what that version needed; its date is that version's. Its source is one opened for this table and checked on the page image, or the row says 'primary not opened' and names what its date was checked against (the Historical Tech Tree has no licence, so it guides checks and is cited by no row). Rows marked alsoRan are lamps Earth built that its ledger does not list. A row with no date is invented for a world, and says so. Written 2026-11-21 by the engine's builder, the measure, the also-rans and the sources by its second pass; read row by row before commit. Known misses: Mediterranean vegetable-oil lamps, al-Razi's kerosene (9th century), coke iron, the Welsbach mantle and the carbide lamp are not rows; only lamps carry a figure, and no row has a quantity.

measure.source: Nordhaus (1996), in Bresnahan and Gordon (eds.), The Economics of New Goods, University of Chicago Press, Table 1.6, 'Labor Price of Light', pp. 52 and 53, read on the page images (the scan's text layer misaligns the table's columns)
measure.rule: A lamp's figure is its series' labor price at the earliest date the table gives for it, the version nearest the one that came into use. The labor price is used, not the cents, because it is the table's own measure across eras: a cent of 1800 and a cent of 1883 are not one unit. A lamp the table does not price carries a gap and ranks below every priced lamp.
measure.uncertain: Tables 1.5 and 1.6 give the oils four times the price per 1,000 lumen-hours that Table 1.2 gives for the same 1855 tests (sperm oil 160.256 against 40.1 cents; other oils 59.441 against 14.9), and kerosene twice (4.036 against 2.0, Table 1.2's kerosene priced in 1870); the pages read do not say why. The engine reads Table 1.6 alone.
columns: labor price, hours of work per 1,000 lumen-hours

ties.why: Coal gas and wood gas are one structure (a fuel heated in a cast-iron retort, known from gas chemistry), so the rule cannot choose between them; the table lists coal gas first because Earth took it.

rows.name: the bright strains

rows.invented: Invented for the world where the fungi came early: its lignin-eating fungi, the land's decomposers for longer, include strains that glow bright enough to read by, and they are grown on wood as a crop. Earth's glowing fungi are far dimmer (foxfire).
